169.title: The example of the wise (3.17–3.29)
169.hook: people copy what you do, not what you say, and Krishna says even he keeps working for that reason
169.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Gita 3.20–3.21, on lokasangraha and on people following the example of the best, when speaking of leadership, parenting and public service, and King Janaka is remembered as the model of a wise person who kept working in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yajna: the wheel of food, rain, offering and action, and the one who only takes. Today, who's watching you turn it.

Spend a day around a small child and you know. They don't do what you tell them. They do what you do. You say be gentle, then slam the cupboard, and guess which one they learn. Offices, teams, families and whole countries work the same way: people watch the person at the front, and they copy. Krishna has just told Arjuna to work as an offering. Now he adds a reason Arjuna hadn't thought of. Even if you didn't need to act, other people need you to.
screen: `THEY DO WHAT YOU DO.` → `PEOPLE WATCH THE ONE IN FRONT.` → `OTHERS NEED YOU TO ACT.`

segments.voice: Krishna begins with the rare person who's already free: someone who delights in the self, is content in the self, has nothing left they need to do. You'd think that person could stop. But look at King Janaka, Krishna says. Janaka was a ruler famous for his wisdom, a sage who never left his throne, and he and others like him reached perfection through action. Then the reason: lokasangraham evapi sampashyan kartum arhasi. Keeping in view the holding-together of the world, you should act. Lokasangraha: the good of the world, the keeping of people together. Then the famous line. Yad yad acharati shreshthas tat tad evetaro janah. Whatever the best person does, others do the same. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. Here Krishna points at himself. There's nothing in all three worlds I have to do, he says, nothing I lack and need to get. And yet I keep acting. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So the wise should act as eagerly as the attached do, but unattached, for the good of the world. And they shouldn't unsettle simpler people who are attached to their work; they should do the work well beside them. One more turn at the end. All actions are carried out by the qualities of nature, the gunas. Only the one confused by ego thinks, I am the doer: ahankara vimudhatma kartaham iti manyate. The wise lead by example, and they don't take the credit.
screen: `JANAKA: A SAGE WHO KEPT HIS THRONE.` · `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLD THE WORLD TOGETHER.` · `WHATEVER THE BEST DO, OTHERS DO.` · `EVEN KRISHNA KEEPS WORKING.` · then, large: `LEAD BY DOING, NOT BY TAKING CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Picture the people who see you most, a child, a younger sibling, a coworker, a friend who's struggling, a stranger on your usual bus, and let their faces come one by one. Ask gently: if they copied exactly what I did yesterday, not what I said, what would they learn? Then pick one small thing you'd be glad for them to copy, and picture yourself doing it in front of them.
Lokasangraha. The good of the world, the holding-together of people. Whatever the best person does, others do the same, so even the free keep working, for the good of the world.
Your line: lead by doing. Even Krishna, with nothing he needs, keeps working. That's day one hundred sixty-nine.

170.title: Desire as the enemy (3.30–3.43)
170.hook: Arjuna asks why people do what they know is wrong, as if pushed by force, and Krishna names the enemy
170.howItsDone: Gita 3.35, better one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well, and 3.37, naming desire and anger as the enemy, are verses some Hindus learn by heart and return to when facing a hard choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lokasangraha: whatever the best do, others do, so even Krishna keeps working. Today, the end of chapter three.

Ten minutes after the text someone swore they wouldn't send, a small question shows up: why did I do that? I knew better. The same question follows the third helping, the thing said in anger, the app opened again at midnight. As if something else had its hands on the wheel. Near the end of chapter three, Arjuna asks exactly this. What pushes a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against their own will, as if forced? Krishna's answer is short, and it names two things.
screen: `WHY DID I DO THAT?` → `SOMETHING ELSE AT THE WHEEL.` → `ARJUNA ASKS IT TOO.`

segments.voice: First Krishna gathers up the chapter: offer all your actions to me, and fight, free of fever. Then verse thirty-five. Shreyan svadharmo vigunah, paradharmat svanushthitat. Better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Someone else's path, however well walked, is full of fear. Then Arjuna's question: atha kena prayukto 'yam papam charati purushah. By what is a person driven to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? Krishna's answer: kama esha krodha esha. It is desire. It is anger. Born of restlessness, the quality called rajas, all-devouring, the great wrong. Know this, he says, as the enemy. Then three pictures of how it hides. As fire is covered by smoke. As a mirror is covered by dust. As a baby is covered by the womb. The light is still there; you just can't see it. This enemy is like a fire that's never satisfied, and it lives in the senses, the mind and the understanding, using them to cloud what you know. So Krishna gives an order of strength. The senses are powerful. The mind is higher than the senses, the understanding higher than the mind, and higher than understanding is the self. Steady yourself by the self, and then: jahi shatrum mahabaho kamarupam durasadam. Strike down, mighty-armed one, this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome. That's chapter three. The action was never the problem. The grasping is.
screen: `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA, IMPERFECT.` · `WHAT DRIVES US, AS IF FORCED?` · `DESIRE AND ANGER: THE ENEMY.` · `SMOKE, DUST, THE WOMB.` · then, large: `STRIKE DOWN THE ENEMY CALLED DESIRE.`

segments.voice: Picture a mirror under a fine layer of dust: that's how a strong want sits over what you already know. Think of one thing you do even though you know better, and name the want underneath it plainly, I want comfort, I want to be right, I want more, without fighting it. With each out-breath, picture one slow wipe across the glass; behind the dust, the mirror was always clear.
Kama. Desire, named with anger as the enemy. What drives us to act against what we know, hiding like smoke over fire, dust over a mirror.
Your line: know the enemy. It hides like smoke over a fire. See you tomorrow.

171.title: "Whenever dharma declines, I come" (4.1–4.8)
171.hook: Arjuna asks how his friend could have taught the sun, and Krishna says who he really is
171.howItsDone: Gita 4.7–4.8, yada yada hi dharmasya, is often recited and is read as a classic statement of the avatara, the divine descent; Vaishnava Hindus often read it with the ten avatars of Vishnu in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kama: desire, smoke over fire, dust over a mirror. Today, chapter four, and Krishna says who he is.

A friend you grew up with mentions, casually, that he taught this same lesson to the sun, ages ago. That's where chapter four begins. This teaching isn't new, Krishna says. I gave it long ago to Vivasvan, the sun, who passed it to Manu, father of humankind in Hindu tradition, and Manu to the king Ikshvaku, and down it went, king to king, until over a long time it was lost. Now I'm giving it back to you, because you're my friend. Arjuna, reasonably, says: wait. You were born recently, and the sun long before. How could you have taught him?
screen: `I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN.` → `KING TO KING, THEN LOST.` → `BUT YOU WERE BORN RECENTLY.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer: many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all; you don't. Then he says what he is. Though I am unborn, my self imperishable, lord of all beings, I come into being through my own power. Then the promise: yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati bharata. Whenever dharma declines. In Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation of the two verses: "When Righteousness Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take Visible shape, and move a man with men, Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back, And setting Virtue on her seat again." The Sanskrit ends sambhavami yuge yuge: I come into being, age after age. This is the root of the avatara, the descent: the divine coming down into the world in a form, again and again, when things go badly wrong. It's how Vaishnava tradition understands Rama and Krishna, and the list of Vishnu's descents: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf Vamana you met at Onam, and more. Hindu schools read these verses differently. Some hear a personal God truly taking a body out of love. Others hear the one reality appearing through its own power, never bound by it. To both, it isn't a promise that bad times won't come. It's about what happens when they do: when the wrong grows strong, the good returns. You heard this on Janmashtami, about a baby born in a prison at midnight. Now you've heard it from his own mouth.
screen: `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `UNBORN, YET I COME INTO BEING.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES.` · `AVATARA: THE DESCENT, AGE AFTER AGE.` · then, large: `WHEN THE WRONG GROWS STRONG, HE RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Think of a time things had gone badly wrong, in your life, your family, the world, and then something good came back you hadn't expected: a person who showed up, a kindness, a turn. Notice you couldn't see it coming from inside the dark part. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's promise, age after age, I come; if not, hold the memory that good has returned before.
Avatara. The descent: the divine taking form in the world, again and again. Whenever dharma declines, Krishna says, I come, age after age.
Your line: he returns. Age after age, when the wrong grows strong. Day one hundred seventy-one, done.

what it means: whenever the right weakens and the wrong grows strong, the divine takes form, to protect the good and set dharma back on its seat.

172.title: Action without attachment (4.9–4.23)
172.hook: the busiest person in the Gita says his work never touches him, and explains how
172.howItsDone: Some Hindus treat Gita 4.18 as a daily discipline: they work fully, try not to cling to the outcome, and often dedicate a task to God before starting it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avatara, the descent: whenever dharma declines, Krishna comes, age after age. Today, why all that acting never binds him.

A nurse on a double shift. A grandmother cooking for twenty. Everything is happening around them, and somehow nothing seems to be happening to them. They're working hard, but they aren't grabbing. Then there's the person who does one small task and carries it around all day: did they like it, will it work, what will people say? Same work, completely different weight. Krishna has just said he comes into the world again and again. Now he says something stranger: all that coming and acting never binds him. And he tells Arjuna how the same can be true of a person.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENING AROUND THEM.` → `NOTHING HAPPENING TO THEM.` → `SAME WORK, DIFFERENT WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Chapter four, verses nine to twenty-three. Krishna begins with himself. Actions don't stain me, he says, because I have no craving for their fruit, and whoever understands that isn't bound by action either. Then he admits this is hard. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused. So he gives a riddle, verse eighteen: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people. Read it slowly. Some people sit perfectly still and are churning inside, grabbing at outcomes all day long. That's action hiding in inaction. Others move fast, doing a hundred things, and inside they're quiet, not clutching. That's inaction in action. The body can be busy while the grip is loose. The next verses describe that person. They give up clinging to the fruit. They're content, depending on nothing. Even fully engaged in work, the text says, they do nothing at all, in the sense that matters. They take what comes, and stay even in success and in failure. And verse twenty-three says their work melts away, without the sticky residue karma usually leaves. Notice what Krishna doesn't say: stop working. Arjuna wanted to walk off the field, and the answer keeps coming back: act. Just act without the hook in you. The work is real. The chain is optional.
screen: `MY ACTIONS DON'T STAIN ME.` · `EVEN THE WISE ARE CONFUSED.` · `INACTION IN ACTION.` · `THE WORK MELTS AWAY.` · then, large: `THE WORK IS REAL. THE CHAIN IS OPTIONAL.`

segments.voice: Think of one task waiting for you, and picture yourself doing it fully, hands and attention on it. Notice what comes along with it, the worry about how it'll turn out or who will see it, and on each out-breath loosen your grip on that part: keep the task, set down the grabbing. If you pray, you can offer the task to Krishna before you begin it.
Akarma. Inaction: seeing it inside action is wise. Doing the work fully, without clutching at its fruit, so the work doesn't bind you.
Your line: free while acting. Your hand on the work, not on the result. Until tomorrow.

a hymn sung at sunrise

173.title: Sacrifice as knowledge (4.24–4.33)
173.hook: the verse many families say before dinner, and a list of a dozen ways to make an offering
173.howItsDone: Some Hindu families, schools and ashrams chant Gita 4.24 (brahmarpanam) as a grace before meals; the idea of offering breath, study and work as yajna shapes daily practice for some.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akarma: action without attachment, a busy body with a loose grip. Today, a fire, and a dinner table.

In some Hindu homes, and in some school dining halls in India, the food is served, everyone waits, and a short Sanskrit verse is chanted before anyone eats. Some children learn it by ear long before they know what it means. Brahmarpanam, it begins. It's a grace before meals, and it comes from Gita chapter four, verse twenty-four. The surprise is what it says. It doesn't thank anyone for the food. It says the food, the eater, the fire and the offering are all one thing. So how did a verse about fire end up at the dinner table?
screen: `THE FOOD IS SERVED. EVERYONE WAITS.` → `BRAHMARPANAM.` → `A VERSE AT THE DINNER TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the old Vedic sacrifice, the yajna, a priest pours ghee into a fire, and the fire carries the offering to the gods. Verse twenty-four turns that scene inside out. The act of offering is Brahman. The offering is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire, which is Brahman. And the one who sees Brahman in the action reaches Brahman. Every part of the ritual is the same reality. So when families chant it over a plate of rice, the meal becomes the fire, the eating becomes the offering. Then Krishna lists the ways people sacrifice, and the list keeps widening. Some offer to the gods. Some offer their senses into the fire of self-control. Some offer their wealth, or austerity, or yoga, or the study of scripture. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. Even breathing can be a sacrifice. Then verse thirty-three ranks them. Better than any offering of things, Krishna says, is the offering of knowledge, because all action ends in knowledge. The fire has moved inside. What burns now isn't ghee; it's ignorance. A few verses later he says it outright: as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns karma to ash. Seeing clearly is itself the offering, and the seeing burns.
screen: `THE FIRE, THE GHEE, THE PRIEST.` · `ALL OF IT IS BRAHMAN.` · `EVEN BREATH CAN BE AN OFFERING.` · `THE OFFERING OF KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE BURNS KARMA.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine makes breathing an offering. Breathe in slowly and think, this is given; breathe out and think, this is given back, with nothing to fix and nothing to earn, and when your mind wanders, come back to the next breath. If you pray, you can offer the breath to God.
Yajna. Sacrifice, offering: the old fire ritual moved inward. Seeing clearly is the highest offering, and the fire it lights burns karma.
Your line: knowledge burns karma. Even a plate of rice can be an offering. That's day one hundred seventy-three.

a prayer of thanks before a meal

Krishna's list includes self-control, wealth, study, yoga and even the breath.

what a scholar hears: verse 24 maps each part of the Vedic yajna (the ladle, the ghee, the fire, the priest) onto Brahman; the fire image returns in 4.37, where knowledge burns all karma to ash.

174.title: Cut the doubt (4.34–4.42)
174.hook: the Gita praises asking questions and warns against doubt in the same breath
174.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn the Gita from a teacher in the spirit of verse 4.34, with respect, questions and service, and the closing call of chapter four, to cut doubt and stand up, is often cited when facing hard decisions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yajna: the fire moved inside, and knowledge burns karma. Today, the end of chapter four.

It's two in the morning, and you're still deciding. Take the job or don't. Send the text or don't. You've made a list of pros and cons, then another list. Every choice looks wrong from some angle. You're not really thinking anymore; you're circling. That's the Arjuna we met on day one of the Gita, bow on the ground, unable to move. Now Krishna closes chapter four with a picture: a sword, and one clean cut. The twist: in the very same passage, he tells Arjuna to ask questions. So which is it?
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING. STILL DECIDING.` → `CIRCLING, NOT THINKING.` → `A SWORD, AND ONE CLEAN CUT.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-four gives the method for learning. Go to those who have seen the truth, Krishna says. Learn by bowing, by questioning and by serving, and they will teach you. Three Sanskrit words: pranipata, the bow; pariprashna, asking all around a thing; seva, service. Asking is built right into the path. Arjuna himself asks question after question for eighteen chapters, and Krishna never scolds him for it. Then the promises. Even if you were the worst of wrongdoers, verse thirty-six says, you would cross over it all on the raft of knowledge. And verse thirty-seven: as a blazing fire turns firewood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all karma to ash. Then the warning, verse forty: the one without faith, always doubting, is lost; for the doubting self there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. So what's the difference between a question and a doubt? A question moves. It wants an answer and will act on one. The doubt Krishna warns about circles forever and keeps you from ever standing up. Its Sanskrit name, samshaya, is the doubt of a mind hung between two sides, never landing on either. So the last verse of chapter four: cut this doubt in your heart, born of not knowing, with the sword of knowledge. Take refuge in yoga. Stand up, Arjuna. Keep the questions. Cut the circling.
screen: `BOW, QUESTION, SERVE.` · `THE RAFT OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `THE DOUBTER FINDS NO HAPPINESS.` · `THE SWORD, AND STAND UP.` · then, large: `KEEP THE QUESTIONS. CUT THE CIRCLING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been circling, not the biggest decision of your life, and ask yourself one real question about it, the kind that has an answer. On an out-breath, picture the circling as a thread, and let it be cut. You don't have to decide right now; just notice the difference between the question and the loop.

Samshaya. Doubt, the mind hung between two sides, never landing on either. Krishna's last words in chapter four: keep asking real questions, but cut the endless circling with the sword of knowledge, and stand up.
Your line: the sword of knowledge. Questions are part of the path. Chapter four, done.

a question asked to a teacher
losing faith in God for good

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means never asking questions.
what it means: ask, and keep asking, but cut the doubt that circles forever and keeps you from standing up.

175.title: Two paths, one goal (5.1–5.12)
175.hook: Arjuna asks for a straight answer: quit the world, or work in it?
175.howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors both paths: some take formal sannyasa and leave household life, while householders practice karma yoga at home and at work; the lotus leaf of Gita 5.10 is a common image for living in the world untouched by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samshaya: chapter four ended with a sword that cuts the circling doubt. Today, the end of the week, and a straight question.

Just tell me plainly: which one is better? That's Arjuna at the top of chapter five, and after this week you can see why. Lead by doing. Know the enemy, desire. He returns, whenever dharma declines. Free while acting. Knowledge burns karma. The sword of knowledge. Act, Krishna says, again and again. But also: knowledge is the highest thing, and the wise renounce. Some of it seems to pull two ways. So Arjuna asks: you've praised giving up action, and you've praised doing it. Which one?
screen: `JUST TELL ME WHICH ONE.` → `A WEEK OF INSTRUCTIONS.` → `ACT. BUT ALSO, RENOUNCE?`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer, verse two: both lead to the highest good. Renunciation, sannyasa, the path of stepping away from action. And karma yoga, the path of action done without attachment. Both work. Then, since Arjuna asked for a ranking, he gives one: of the two, the yoga of action is better, because, verse six says, real renunciation is hard to reach without it. And verse three redefines the renouncer anyway: know as a constant renouncer the one who neither hates nor craves. The verse says nothing about leaving home. You could be that person with a job and a mortgage. Verse four: only children, not the wise, talk as if the path of knowledge and the path of yoga were different; whoever truly stands on one reaches the fruit of both. Verse five: the place the renouncers reach is reached by those who act too, and the one who sees them as one, sees. Then verse ten gives a picture.
